epithet: Dhat al-Nitaqayn (She of the Two Belts)
role: Provider of food and supplies during the Hijrah of the Prophet ﷺ
Mother of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr
summary: Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) was the daughter of the first Caliph Abu Bakr and elder sister of Aisha (RA). She earned the title 'She of the Two Belts' for tearing her belt in two to seal the provisions she prepared for the Prophet ﷺ and her father during the Hijrah. She lived to approximately 100 years old, witnessing the entire Umayyad period, and died shortly after her son Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was martyred.
biography:
Asma bint Abi Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah al-Qurashiyyah was born in Makkah around 595 CE, approximately twenty-seven years before the Hijrah. She was the daughter of Abu Bakr by his first wife Qutaylah bint Abd al-Uzza, making her the full sister of Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr and the half-sister of Aisha bint Abi Bakr (RA). From her father she inherited his sharp intelligence and his unstinting commitment to the Prophet ﷺ.

Asma was among the early Muslims in Makkah, accepting Islam while the community was still small and under persecution. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' that she accepted Islam as one of the earliest women to do so, and that approximately seventeen or eighteen women had accepted Islam before the Prophet ﷺ emigrated to Abyssinia.

Her most celebrated contribution came at the time of the Hijrah in 622 CE. When the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr were preparing to leave Makkah secretly for Madinah, Asma prepared their provisions — food and water for the journey. She needed to seal the provisions bags but had nothing to tie them with. Without hesitation, she tore her own belt (nitaq) into two pieces and used them to bind the bags. The Prophet ﷺ saw this act and gave her the name 'Dhat al-Nitaqayn' — She of the Two Belts — a title that became her most famous epithet and is recorded in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. The classical commentators note that this title was understood as an honor, because through that act of sacrifice she had earned a metaphorical double belt of Allah's reward.

During the tense days of the Hijrah, Asma also regularly carried food to the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr in the Cave of Thawr, where they were hiding, taking indirect routes to avoid detection by the Quraysh who were searching for them. Ibn Hisham records that she was harassed during this period — Abu Jahl reportedly struck her on one occasion when he came to Abu Bakr's house demanding to know where the Prophet ﷺ had gone. She refused to reveal anything.

Asma subsequently emigrated to Madinah. She married al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA) — one of the ten promised Paradise — and she described their early years in Madinah as one of hardship and manual labor. In a famous narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, she described how she collected date pits to feed al-Zubayr's horse, carried loads of firewood on her head from a long distance, baked bread and drew water, until the Prophet ﷺ came across her one day struggling with a load. The Prophet ﷺ attempted to help her onto a camel, but she felt shy in the presence of other men. When she told al-Zubayr, he said he was more embarrassed by her carrying loads than by her riding on a camel with strangers nearby — a tender exchange preserved across the centuries.

Asma was the mother of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (RA), who was the first Muslim child born in Madinah after the Hijrah — a fact celebrated by the early community as an end to an evil omen spread by the Jews of Madinah that no children would be born to the Muslim emigrants. The Prophet ﷺ performed the tahnik (rubbing of chewed date on the newborn's palate) for Abd Allah himself — one of the highest honors for an infant in that era.

Asma lived to an extraordinary age — most classical sources say she reached approximately 100 years without losing her mental faculties and without her teeth falling out. She outlived nearly all of the Companions. Al-Dhahabi marvels at her longevity in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'.

The final chapter of her life was marked by grief. Her son Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr had established himself as a rival caliph to the Umayyads and held Makkah for years before being besieged and killed by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf's forces in 73 AH (692 CE). When Abd Allah was brought to her after his death, she is reported to have said with extraordinary composure: 'Has this horseman dismounted?' She had already counseled him earlier: 'Die nobly, do not allow them to slay you while you are fleeing.' Ibn Kathir records her final conversation with her son before the battle in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah as one of the most moving in Islamic history. Asma died days after her son, in the same year 73 AH, at an age of approximately one hundred years.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam among the early converts in Makkah
Prepared provisions for the Hijrah and tore her belt in two — earned the title 'Dhat al-Nitaqayn'
Carried food secretly to the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hiding in the Cave of Thawr
Emigrated to Madinah; married al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA)
Gave birth to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr — first Muslim child born in Madinah after the Hijrah; Prophet ﷺ performed tahnik
Her son Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was killed by al-Hajjaj; Asma died days later at approximately age 100

notable_traits: Courageous under direct threat — refused to reveal the Prophet's whereabouts to Abu Jahl
Practical and resourceful — prepared provisions for the Hijrah from her own household
Remarkable endurance — worked physically hard in early Madinah despite her father being the wealthiest Muslim
Extraordinary longevity — approximately 100 years old at death, with faculties intact
Composed and dignified in grief — her final counsel to her son before his martyrdom is recorded as exemplary
narrated_hadith_count: approximately 58 hadith in the major collections
